metadata.title: Adolescents' expected civic participation: The role of civic knowledge and efficacy beliefs

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses ICCS 2009 microdata for a nationally representative sample of Italian eighth-grade students, sampled via a stratified two-stage probability design (schools as primary sampling units and one full class of eighth graders randomly selected within each sampled school). Because of the complex student sampling structure, the authors state that appropriate sampling weights were applied in the analysis (Schulz et al., 2011). The paper does not report a specific weight variable name in the provided text, but it explicitly justifies weighting for the ICCS design. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is described, and the analysis is conducted with MPlus using a robust estimator suitable for sampling weights.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants are 3352 Italian eighth-grade students who took part in the IEA ICCS 2009 assessment. The sampling procedure is a stratified two-stage probability design: 172 schools are sampled from the population of Italian lower secondary schools, and one full class of eighth graders is randomly selected in each school. The paper states that the amount of missing data is small (approximately 0.2%–2.6%) and is handled via expectation-maximization; no additional exclusion criteria (e.g., minimum item completion) are described in the provided text. Data collection occurred in classrooms during an ordinary school day using the ICCS cognitive test and student questionnaire following the IEA assessment protocol.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ICCS 2009 the study leveraged Socioeconomic background (NISB), Internal political efficacy, Citizenship self-efficacy to predict Primary study outcome (heuristic migration), finding that This study analyzes ICCS 2009 data for Italian eighth-grade students (N=3352) to explain adolescents’ expected civic participation using a measurement-and-structural modeling framework. Expected civic participation is operationalized as a latent construct indicated by four questionnaire indices: expected electoral participation, expected political activities, expected informal political participation, and expected legal protest. Civic knowledge is measured with a 79-item ICCS test spanning civic society/systems, principles, participation, identities, and knowing/reasoning/analysis; five plausible-value estimates are generated and used as indicators in the model. The authors report good measurement-model fit (CFA: χ²(2)=21.954; CFI=.991; RMSEA=.055; SRMR=.013) and acceptable structural-model fit (SEM: χ²(200)=1921.092; CFI=.954; RMSEA=.051; SRMR=.058), with the model explaining 61% of variance in expected civic participation. Missing data are handled via expectation-maximization, and sampling weights are applied due to the ICCS stratified two-stage design. Limitations include the cross-sectional design (no causal claims) and the absence of ML predictive modeling; results are based on SEM path estimates rather than algorithmic prediction metrics. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is not an empirical machine-learning prediction/classification study. It uses CFA/SEM with plausible values and expectation-maximization for missingness, but it does not train or compare ML algorithms, so ml_techniques are intentionally empty and main_findings are not populated under the ML schema. The outcome is modeled via latent-variable structural paths rather than ML performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE), and therefore the ML-specific fields (main_findings with predictive metrics) are not applicable to this extraction template.
